flashcards.q: Does recursion depth in DFS correspond to the total number of nodes, or to something else?
flashcards.a: Recursion depth equals the tree's height (or the longest path DFS descends before backtracking), NOT total node count. A balanced million-node tree recurses ~20 levels deep; a degenerate linked-list-shaped million-node tree recurses a million levels deep.

flashcards.q: Converting a recursive DFS to iterative -- does this improve the Big-O space complexity?
flashcards.a: No. Both forms use O(H) auxiliary space where H is the height/longest path. The real benefit is moving that O(H) footprint from the call stack (small, fixed size, e.g. Python's ~1000-frame default limit) to the heap (much larger, elastic) -- it avoids a hard resource ceiling, it doesn't change the asymptotic bound.

flashcards.q: Why does directed-cycle detection (Course Schedule, LC207) require THREE states per node instead of a single visited flag?
flashcards.a: A single visited flag can't distinguish 'this node is an ancestor of the current node on the active call stack' (a real cycle) from 'this node was already fully explored via a different, unrelated branch' (normal in a DAG with shared dependencies, e.g. diamond-shaped A->B->D, A->C->D). Collapsing these produces false-positive cycle detection on valid DAGs.

flashcards.q: In iterative preorder DFS using an explicit stack, which child must you push first, and why?
flashcards.a: Push the RIGHT child first, then the LEFT child. Since a stack is LIFO, pushing right first means left ends up on top and gets popped/processed first, preserving the expected left-before-right traversal order.

flashcards.q: What is the reliable trick for producing postorder traversal iteratively without fiddly state tracking?
flashcards.a: Do an iterative 'root, right, left' traversal (which is just preorder with the child-push order swapped), then reverse the resulting output list. Reversing 'root, right, left' yields exactly 'left, right, root' -- true postorder.

flashcards.q: In Path Sum II (collecting all root-to-leaf paths matching a target sum), why must you record a COPY of the path list at a match, not a reference to the live list?
flashcards.a: The shared path list continues being mutated (appended and popped) as the DFS continues exploring other branches after this leaf returns. Storing a live reference means every recorded 'path' ends up reflecting whatever the list looks like at the very end of the whole traversal, not what it looked like at the moment of the match.

flashcards.q: Why can a recursive Number of Islands solution be a real production risk on a very large grid, even though it's algorithmically correct?
flashcards.a: A single connected component (island) shaped as a long winding snake across a 10,000 x 10,000 grid can recurse on the order of 10^7-10^8 calls along that path, far past any default call-stack limit, crashing with a stack overflow -- it must be converted to iterative DFS/BFS with an explicit heap-allocated stack/queue for safety at that scale.

flashcards.q: In Clone Graph, why is a visited-to-clone MAP required instead of a plain visited SET?
flashcards.a: A plain set only tells you whether a node has been seen, not WHICH clone object corresponds to it. Without the map, you can't correctly wire a neighbor reference to the one true corresponding clone, and you risk creating duplicate clones of the same original node.

flashcards.q: Why is checking only 'each node's value against its immediate parent' insufficient to validate a Binary Search Tree (LC98)?
flashcards.a: A BST's ordering constraint is global across every ancestor on the path to the root, not just the direct parent. A correct recursive solution must thread an evolving (low, high) bound down through the recursion, since a node deep in a subtree must respect bounds set by ancestors several levels up, not merely its immediate parent.

flashcards.q: How does computing the Diameter of a Binary Tree (LC543) in one O(n) postorder pass avoid the O(n^2) naive approach?
flashcards.a: The naive approach recomputes height as a separate recursive call at every node, costing up to O(n) per node in a skewed tree, O(n^2) total. The efficient approach computes height AND updates a global best-diameter (left_height + right_height at each node) within the SAME single postorder pass, since height is already being computed bottom-up anyway.
